title: AI and Machine Learning
description: The core ideas of machine learning: supervised and unsupervised learning, linear and logistic regression, gradient descent, overfitting, neural networks and how to evaluate models.

lessons.title: What Machine Learning Is
objectives: Define machine learning in one sentence
Name features, labels and a model
lessons.body:
Machine learning builds programs that improve at a task by learning from data instead of following hand-written rules. You provide examples, an algorithm adjusts the parameters of a model, and the trained model makes predictions on new data.

In supervised learning every training example has a label, the correct answer, so the model learns a mapping from features (the inputs) to labels. If the label is a number, such as a house price, the task is regression; if it is a category, such as spam or not spam, it is classification.

In unsupervised learning there are no labels and the algorithm looks for structure, for example grouping similar customers with clustering. A third family, reinforcement learning, learns from rewards while interacting with an environment. Most beginner projects use supervised learning.

definitions.meaning: An input variable used to make a prediction.
The correct output for a training example.
A function with adjustable parameters that maps features to predictions.
Adjusting model parameters to fit the data.

lessons.example:
# supervised data
X = [[50], [80], [120]]   # area in m2 (feature)
y = [150, 240, 360]       # price in thousands (label)
# regression: learn price from area
lessons.exampleNote: Each row of X has a matching label in y. A regression model learns the relation, here roughly price = 3 x area.
lessons.diagram:
data + labels --> [ training ]
                        |
                      model
                        |
  new input ------> prediction
mistakes: Using test data during training: keep it separate to measure honestly.
Thinking more data always fixes a bad model: quality and features matter.
Calling any program with if-statements machine learning.

practice.a: The correct answer attached to a training example.
Unsupervised, because it uses no labels.

exercises: List three supervised and three unsupervised tasks.
Decide whether predicting tomorrow's temperature is regression or classification.
summary: Supervised uses labels; unsupervised does not.
Regression predicts numbers, classification predicts categories.

lessons.title: Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
objectives: Write the model y = w x + b
Perform one gradient-descent update by hand
lessons.body:
Linear regression fits a straight line y = w x + b to data. The weight w is the slope and b is the intercept. To measure how good a line is, we use a loss function; the usual choice is mean squared error (MSE), the average of (prediction minus target) squared.

Gradient descent finds good parameters by repeating small steps. The gradient tells us how the loss changes with each parameter, and we move the parameter in the opposite direction: w = w - lr x dLoss/dw. The learning rate lr sets the step size. Too large and the loss may bounce or diverge; too small and learning is slow.

For MSE with one feature and no bias, dLoss/dw = (2/n) x sum((w x - y) x).

definitions.meaning: Mean of squared differences between predictions and targets.
Vector of partial derivatives showing how the loss changes with each parameter.
Size of each gradient-descent step.
One full pass over the training data.

lessons.exampleNote: The negative gradient says increasing w lowers the loss, so w moves from 0 up to 1.0. More steps would approach 2.
lessons.diagram:
loss
   |\
   | \        o start
   |  \     o
   |   \  o
   |    \o  <- steps downhill
   +------*--------- w
mistakes: Using a huge learning rate: the loss may increase instead of decrease.
Forgetting to scale features: gradient descent can be slow.
Adding the gradient instead of subtracting it.

practice.q: Which way do we move parameters in gradient descent?
practice.a: Against the gradient, to reduce the loss.

practice.q: What does a too-large learning rate cause?
practice.a: Overshooting, so the loss may oscillate or diverge.

exercises: Do a second update step from w = 1.0 with the same data.
Explain why MSE squares the differences.
summary: Linear regression fits y = w x + b.
Gradient descent steps against the gradient scaled by the learning rate.

lessons.title: Classification and Logistic Regression
objectives: Explain how the sigmoid turns a score into a probability
Describe what a decision boundary is
lessons.body:
Logistic regression is a classification method despite its name. It first computes a linear score z = w x + b, then passes it through the sigmoid function, sigmoid(z) = 1 / (1 + e^-z), which squeezes any number into the range 0 to 1. The result is read as the probability of the positive class.

To get a class label we apply a threshold, commonly 0.5. If the probability is at least the threshold we predict the positive class. A different threshold trades one kind of error for another.

The points where the model is exactly undecided (probability 0.5, which means z = 0) form the decision boundary. The loss usually used for training is cross-entropy, which punishes confident wrong predictions heavily.

definitions.meaning: Function 1/(1+e^-z) mapping any number to a value between 0 and 1.
Probability above which the positive class is predicted.
Where the model is undecided: probability 0.5.
Loss that penalises confident wrong probabilities.

lessons.example:
z = 2.0 -> sigmoid(2) = 1/(1+e^-2) = 0.881 -> predict positive
z = 0.0 -> sigmoid(0) = 0.5   -> on the boundary
z = -1.0 -> sigmoid(-1) = 0.269 -> predict negative
lessons.exampleNote: Large positive scores give probabilities near 1, large negative ones near 0, and z = 0 gives exactly 0.5.
mistakes: Treating the output as a guaranteed label: it is a probability until thresholded.
Always using 0.5 even when one error type costs more.
Using accuracy alone on very imbalanced data.

practice.q: What is the decision boundary of logistic regression?
practice.a: The set of inputs where z = 0, i.e. probability 0.5.

exercises: Explain what raising the threshold to 0.8 does to predictions.
summary: A threshold turns probabilities into classes.

lessons.title: Overfitting, Bias and Variance
objectives: Use train, validation and test sets correctly
Name two ways to reduce overfitting
lessons.body:
A model should perform well on data it has never seen. Overfitting happens when a model learns the training data too closely, including its noise, so training error is low but error on new data is high. Underfitting is the opposite: the model is too simple to capture the pattern, so error is high everywhere.

Bias is error from overly simple assumptions; variance is error from sensitivity to the particular training set. Simple models tend to have high bias and low variance, complex models the reverse, so there is a trade-off.

To measure generalization we split the data into a training set to fit the model, a validation set to choose settings, and a test set used once at the end. Overfitting can be reduced with more data, simpler models, regularization (penalising large weights), early stopping and cross-validation.

definitions.meaning: Fitting noise in the training data, which hurts performance on new data.
A model too simple to capture the pattern.
Held-out data used to tune model choices.
Adding a penalty to discourage overly complex models.

lessons.example:
train error 2%, validation error 25%  -> overfitting
train error 30%, validation error 31% -> underfitting
train error 5%,  validation error 6%  -> good fit
lessons.exampleNote: A large gap between training and validation error signals overfitting. Both being high signals underfitting.
mistakes: Tuning on the test set: it then stops being an honest estimate.
Judging a model only by training accuracy.
Adding complexity when the real issue is too little data.

practice.a: Low training error but much higher validation error.

practice.q: What is the test set for?
practice.a: A final, one-time estimate of performance on unseen data.

exercises: Sketch the learning curve for an overfit model.
Name two ways to reduce overfitting.
summary: Overfit = great on training, poor on new data.
Use train, validation and test sets.
Regularization, more data and simpler models help.

lessons.title: Neural Networks and Backpropagation
objectives: Compute the output of one neuron
Explain what an activation function does
lessons.body:
A neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, z = w1 x1 + w2 x2 + ... + b, and then applies an activation function. Without activations, a stack of layers would collapse into a single linear function. Common activations are ReLU, which outputs max(0, z), and the sigmoid.

A neural network arranges neurons in layers: an input layer, one or more hidden layers and an output layer. The forward pass pushes data through the layers to produce a prediction, and a loss compares it with the label.

Backpropagation computes how the loss changes with every weight by applying the chain rule from the output back to the input. Gradient descent then updates the weights. Networks with many hidden layers are called deep. The details of training large models are beyond this lesson.

definitions.meaning: Computes a weighted sum plus bias and applies an activation.
A non-linear function applied to a neuron's sum.
Computing the network output from the inputs.
Computing gradients layer by layer with the chain rule.

lessons.exampleNote: The same sum gives different outputs depending on the activation: ReLU outputs 0 while sigmoid outputs about 0.27.
lessons.diagram:
x1 --w1--\
            (sum + b) -> f -> out
  x2 --w2--/
  hidden layers repeat this
  forward ----->   loss
  <----- gradients (backprop)
mistakes: Leaving out activation functions: layers then collapse into one linear map.
Initialising all weights to the same value so neurons learn the same thing.
Thinking backprop is a separate learning method: it computes gradients for gradient descent.

practice.q: What does ReLU output for z = -3?

practice.a: The gradient of the loss with respect to each weight.

exercises: Compute the neuron output with weights [1, 1], bias -1 and inputs [0.5, 0.5] using ReLU.
Explain why an activation function is needed.
summary: Neuron = weighted sum + bias, then activation.
Forward pass predicts; backprop supplies gradients.
Non-linear activations make deep networks powerful.

lessons.title: Evaluating Models: Precision, Recall, F1
objectives: Compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1
Choose a metric for imbalanced data
lessons.body:
A confusion matrix counts predictions in four boxes: true positives (TP), false positives (FP), false negatives (FN) and true negatives (TN).

Accuracy = (TP + TN) / all. Precision = TP / (TP + FP) answers: of the items predicted positive, how many were right? Recall = TP / (TP + FN) answers: of the real positives, how many did we find? F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, 2PR / (P + R), and is high only when both are high.

Accuracy can mislead when classes are imbalanced. A model that always says not fraud is 99 percent accurate if only 1 percent of cases are fraud, yet it finds none. In such cases look at precision, recall or F1.

definitions.meaning: TP / (TP + FP): how many predicted positives were correct.
TP / (TP + FN): how many actual positives were found.
Harmonic mean of precision and recall.
Data where one class is much rarer than another.

lessons.exampleNote: The model is right 85 percent of the time, but it finds only two thirds of the real positives.
lessons.diagram:
predicted
             pos     neg
 actual pos   TP      FN
 actual neg   FP      TN
mistakes: Quoting accuracy alone on imbalanced data.
Mixing up precision and recall: precision looks at predictions, recall looks at real positives.
Forgetting that raising the threshold usually raises precision and lowers recall.
exercises: Compute recall and F1 for TP=30, FP=10, FN=30.
Explain which metric matters most for a cancer screening test.
summary: Confusion matrix: TP, FP, FN, TN.
Precision, recall and F1 describe positives.
